extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for piano practice, technique, teaching, tone production, and interpretation drawn from interviews with master pianists and teachers. Focused on how to train, evaluate, and develop pianistic skill and teaching methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legato, slow study, and deep touch for tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Paderewski 'lays great stress on legato playing, and desires everything to be studied slowly, with deep touch and with full, clear tone.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study slowly to produce legato; focus on deep touch and full clear tone. Example exercise: press the hand against the keyboard while the wrist remains low and motionless and let each finger draw out as much tone as possible. Caution: take care with this tonic to avoid 'lameness' if misused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scales and arpeggios with accents to build evenness
rubrics_metrics.description: Study scales and arpeggios with accents (e.g., accent every third note) to enable each finger in turn to make the accent impulse and secure evenness of touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use varied accents, rhythms and tonal dynamics in scales; include arpeggios. Czerny Op. 740 and Clementi's Gradus recommended as technical material. Scales in double thirds and sixths used later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide difficult double passages for separate practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Double passages, such as double thirds and sixths, should be divided and each half practised separately, with legato touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice each hand/half independently until secure; then combine. This prevents overwhelming coordination errors and builds accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Octave practice technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Octaves should be practised with loose wrists and staccato touch; as a preparatory study practise with thumb alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both weight and crisp staccato methods: practise octaves slowly using weight, or faster with crisp staccato. Metronome and repeated patterns (e.g., four repetitions per note) help velocity. Sit low at the piano aids octave execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thumb shape and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: The thumb must always be kept curved, with joints well rounded out; it should touch the keys with its tip, so as to keep it on a level with the other fingers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be very particular about thumb; maintain tip contact and curvature to ensure evenness and avoid awkward hand position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of tonal color and strong contrasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Require all possible variety in tone production. He likes strong contrasts, which are brought out, not only by variety of touch but by skilful use of the pedals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop intent listening to judge shades of tone; use pedal and touch combinations to create color. Adapt tone production to hall size (more effort in large halls).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and distinctness of utterance
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinctness of utterance is of prime importance. The fingers must be rendered firm, with no giving in at the nail joint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train fingers with up-and-down movements while wrist held low and pressed against keyboard; avoid vague, imagined effects—produce clear audible results. Use exercises and Czerny material to build firmness. Critique anti-pattern: feeling you're producing effects when they are not audible to listeners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent fingering
rubrics_metrics.description: Once fingering is decided upon it must be kept to. Employ a fingering which is most comfortable to the hand, as well as one which, in the long run, will render the passage most effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose fingering that suits the hand and tonal result; be sensitive as each finger can produce a different quality. Avoid slavish adherence to editions that over-elaborate (e.g., Von Buelow editions criticized as pedantic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate, economical motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Elimination of every unnecessary movement, yet the whole body should be free and supple. Motions should be as carefully studied as other technical points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study gestures and arm movements; large movements must have dramatic significance and be controlled so hand returns to ready position. Anti-pattern: flopping hands or uncontrolled large movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt practice to performance space
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone production varies according to the space which is to be filled. Greater effort must be put forth in a large hall to make the tone carry, render the touch clear, accents decisive and contrasts pronounced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simulate hall conditions (e.g., keep studio piano lid closed) and strengthen touch accordingly. Practice power and projection selectively rather than always at full force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation through detailed dissection
rubrics_metrics.description: A great artist's performance ought to sound like a spontaneous improvisation, but to achieve this the composition must be dissected in minutest detail; inspiration followed by painstaking work until the ideal is realized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work out all details after forming an initial conception. Maintain a consistent conception across performances—Paderewski argued an artist ought to play 'in the same way' to express his ideal. Anti-pattern: assuming spontaneity replaces preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individualized technical routine
rubrics_metrics.description: Technic is such an individual matter—it depends on physique, mentality, amount of nervous energy, the hand and wrist. Only a few general rules fit most cases; after foundational training one must work out things for oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should tailor exercises to each pupil's strengths/weaknesses (e.g., wrists vs fingers). Avoid one-size-fits-all routines; diagnose problems and prescribe specific remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the metronome to build velocity gradually
rubrics_metrics.description: To attain velocity the best means is to work with the metronome; one can't jump at once into necessary agility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase tempo incrementally while maintaining control and firmness; combine with specific exercises (trills, octaves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with exact finger movements before weight touch
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a mistake to begin study by imitating an artist's weight playing; very exact finger movements must be learned in the beginning before adopting weight touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundational training should emphasize precise finger action; only later incorporate arm weight and other modified touches. Anti-pattern: beginners attempting to emulate mature artists' economy of motion without foundational skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold memorization: eye, ear, and hand
rubrics_metrics.description: Memorizing piano music can be accomplished in three ways: with the eye (mental photograph of the notes), with the ear (mental hearing), and with the hand (physical practice until automatic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine reading, mental hearing, and keyboard practice. Practice small portions intensely away from the piano as needed; mental rehearsal and recitation aid memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration as the keynote of mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentration: without that, little of value can be accomplished. Intense, focused practice accomplishes far more than unthinking repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop the power of attention; when pupils lack concentration, use very slow reading and deliberate attention to single notes/phrases to awaken focused thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relaxation of arms, wrist and shoulders
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless relaxation is present in arms, wrist and shoulders, the tone will be hard and the whole performance constrained and unmusical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt athletic poise, physical exercises (light dumb-bells) emphasizing one muscle at a time. Relaxation prevents fatigue and instrument damage. Practice relaxed techniques and monitor for stiffness or pain as signals of incorrect technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher as diagnostician and individual prescriber
rubrics_metrics.description: The teacher's work is both corrective and constructive: he must see what is wrong and be able to correct it, finding weak parts and building them up with remedies that fit each pupil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose hand, wrist, mentality and craft individualized plans (e.g., more wrist practice for feeble wrists, tone exercises for those with limited tonal ideas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in use of etudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Give very few etudes, and those administered in homeopathic doses; much technique may be learned from pieces themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer musical pieces supplemented by targeted technical work; avoid overloading students with etude mass which can be counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep repertoire by teaching and mental review
rubrics_metrics.description: A pianist who teaches keeps up repertoire; for new programs mentally go over pieces, though experienced artists may not need extensive mental review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use teaching assignments and mental practice to retain a large repertoire. Be aware of the risk that teacherly recollections of students' mistakes can intrude during performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exhausting full-force practice; conserve energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Conserving vital energy in practice: wrong to continually practise the piece as though playing in public with all energy and emotion; practice should not always be full tone to avoid waste and fatigue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice with medium tone and indicate effects rather than always performing at forte. Reserve full-force rehearsals for occasional checks and performance preparation. Aim to be able to practise many hours without fatigue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent listening: listen to each tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The ear tests and judges each shade and quality of tone; students must listen to each tone they produce for quality and variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate critical acoustic self-monitoring; teachers should train pupils to hear intended effects and compare to produced sound. Use listening to guide tone production and finger adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of different touches depending on stylistic aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Different players use different parts of the finger—tip, ball, or almost flat hand—to achieve various tone qualities; most agree on employing arm weight in playing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore multiple touch techniques (end of finger, ball, flat hand) to achieve desired tone; adapt to repertoire and teacher's aims. Study examples: Busoni (end of finger), Cortot (hand almost flat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulate performance conditions selectively
rubrics_metrics.description: During daily practise one often does not need to play forte nor use the pedals; full performance conditions should be used at intervals only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate effects in routine practice and reserve full run-throughs for rehearsal sessions to avoid wasting energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical posture and seating height
rubrics_metrics.description: A low seat at the piano is a necessity for certain practices; sitting low is an aid to weight playing and helps some technical approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust bench height and body alignment to suit the technical method being trained (e.g., low seat for weight techniques, but be aware it may be harder to obtain results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about improvising to cover memory lapses
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvising on a well-known work to fill a forgotten passage is rather a dangerous thing to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ad-hoc improvisation in performance to 'fix' memory lapses; favor thorough memorization and prepared alternative passages if necessary. Anecdote: constructing a bridge can risk losing whether original or improvised material was played.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone development exercises and preparatory work away from piano
rubrics_metrics.description: For students with poor touch, go back to first principles: learn correct movements and conditions of hands, arms and fingers, and these can be acquired at a table; also give simple music to play so tonal sense is not neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use off-piano exercises to build correct anatomy and movement; concurrently use simple melodic pieces (Schubert, Chopin) to develop tonal quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical, unthinking repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeating a technical illustration hundreds of times without thought is largely useless; mental involvement is necessary for improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentionally couple repetitions with focused thought and diagnosis of errors; practice with purpose and variability rather than rote repetition.
